claims.text: A sputtered CrN film will improve the molten-aluminum corrosion resistance of boride-based components relative to uncoated borides.
A pre-sputtered Cr buffer layer can improve adhesion of the CrN film to the substrate.
As-fabricated boride components are vulnerable to direct molten-aluminum attack and interfacial degradation during hot-dip plating.
Sputtered CrN develops a columnar grain microstructure.
The deposited CrN layer is dense.
The CrN layer limits wetting by molten aluminum.
The CrN layer reduces interdiffusion between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
The CrN coating acts as a physical and chemical barrier between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
Preventing direct aluminum-substrate contact limits penetration and reactive dissolution of the boride.
CrN has a low wetting angle with molten aluminum.
A low wetting angle minimizes aluminum film formation along the interface and thereby reduces corrosion damage.
CrN-coated borides will exhibit less mass loss than bare borides during molten-aluminum exposure.
CrN-coated borides will exhibit lower corrosion-current density than bare borides.
Increasing CrN sputtering time and film thickness can improve corrosion resistance.
Untreated boride components typically exhibit higher mass loss and surface degradation due to molten-aluminum attack.
The coating will remain effective during repeated high-temperature plating cycles if it remains intact and adherent.
Mechanical wear or severe thermal cycling that compromises the CrN film will diminish its protective effect.
Protection requires operation within the thermal-stability range of CrN.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator says CrN limits molten-aluminum wetting, but the mechanism attributes protection to a low wetting angle. A lower contact angle conventionally indicates greater wetting, so the stated wetting mechanism is internally inconsistent unless a different angle convention is explicitly defined.
